19665-my-lady-of-the-chinese-courtyard:
A writer on China was once asked why so little was written about Chinese women. He answered that one never hears about them. My Lady of the Chinese Courtyard answers that silence. It presents the life of a Chinese lady from inside her courtyard home. The book came to Western readers as letters and intimate domestic scenes.

Domestic writing of this kind gave foreign readers a rare view. Women's lives in old China were mostly hidden from print. A courtyard view shows family rank, ritual, and daily care up close. It also shows the limits of what an outsider could see. The book survives as a window into a closed world, opened a crack.
19902-the-affectionate-shepherd:
Richard Barnfield published The Affectionate Shepherd in 1594. It is a pastoral poem of a shepherd's love, among England's earliest such works. This edition's notes trace Barnfield's other writings. They list his lament for Lady Pecunia and The Encomium of Lady Pecunia. Copies sit in the British Museum and the Ashmolean. The scholarship around the poem is part of this volume's matter.

Barnfield was a contemporary and admirer of Shakespeare. Some once credited his sonnets to Shakespeare himself. The Affectionate Shepherd sings Daphnis's longing in rich pastoral dress. Its homoerotic frankness startled later centuries of editors. The poem holds a real place in Elizabethan literature. This old edition shows scholars recovering it.
19904-the-noble-lord:
Percival Wilde wrote The Noble Lord as a comedy in one act. Its stage business opens with a drenched handkerchief. The hero draws it from a hip pocket, wetter than his hands. He throws it away with vexation. Then he kneels by an unconscious girl and lays his ear over her heart. He looks quizzical, then rather timid. Wilde packs a rescue, a mystery, and a romance into minutes.

One-act plays fed vaudeville bills and amateur stages alike. Wilde was a master of the short form. A lord, a girl, and a wet evening supply his machinery. Timing matters more than scenery in such pieces. The Noble Lord shows his economy at work. It is theater built for one set and quick laughs.
20423-joyous-gard:
Joyous Gard takes its name and spirit from the Arthurian legends of Sir Lancelot. Its pages draw on the old romance of the Round Table. One passage retells the end of Lancelot's life, when a bishop finds him at peace.

The bishop explains his mirth: Lancelot was with him, with more angels than he ever saw men upon one day. So, the old story says, it was well with that great knight at the last. Around such scenes the book builds quiet essays on courage, joy, and the well-kept life, using the legends as a mirror.
20862-jerry-s-reward:
Jefferson Square, one short block in Gaminsville, holds a convent and a dumping common. Evelyn Snead Barnett sets Jerry's Reward, from 1900, in that tight world. A high brick wall guards the Convent of the Good Shepherd on its large lot.

Jerry, a street boy of the square, stands at the tale's warm centre. Kind deeds and their just reward shape the plot in classic form. Barnett wrote tales that found grace in rough city corners. This one shows her touch: slum scenes drawn with care, and a boy whose good heart earns more than coin by the close.
21328-the-parables-of-our-lord:
The Reverend William Arnot published this study of the parables of Jesus in London in 1874 with T. Nelson and Sons. Arnot also wrote Laws from Heaven for Life on Earth, a study of Proverbs, and Roots and Fruits of the Christian Life. His parables book works through the stories Jesus told, one by one.

Arnot writes for ordinary Christian readers rather than scholars, opening each parable's setting, meaning, and use in daily life. The seed, the soils, the lost sheep, and the talents become lessons in faith and conduct. His preface looks back warmly on the Reformers and Puritans as models of plain, serious Bible teaching for the home.
21448-the-african-trader-or-the-adventur:
Harry Bayford loses his father and his ease at the start of W. H. G. Kingston's The African Trader. Harry was born in Jamaica, where his father was a West India merchant, and schooled in England. Business losses break the father's health, and he dies.

Rather than burden his sisters, Harry ships on a trading vessel bound for Africa. Yellow fever kills much of the crew, and fire takes the ship on the way home. Harry and an African seaman escape on a raft, only to be picked up by a slave trader. A Royal Navy warship then gives chase, with lives in the balance.
22232-the-carved-cupboard:
Amy Le Feuvre, author of Teddy's Button and Probable Sons, published The Carved Cupboard in 1899. Le Feuvre wrote religious tales for children that sold in the millions. Her story opens with a supplanter and four verses, then moves to a country home. Clare, one of her girls, toys with her spoon at tea, listening with half her mind while her thoughts wander elsewhere.

A carved cupboard, nicknamed Bluebeard's cupboard in one chapter, holds the family's secret. Sealed directions in an envelope hang over the plot like a will. Le Feuvre mixes mystery with her usual lessons of faith and patience. The book is a fair piece of her gentle, popular art.
22536-jane-austen-her-life-and-letters-a:
William Austen-Leigh wrote Jane Austen: Her Life and Letters as a family record. He was the novelist's great-nephew, working with family papers. New documents became available for this fuller account of her life.

Miss Jane Austen, granddaughter of Admiral Charles Austen, allowed generous access. Miss Margaret Bellas, great-granddaughter of James Austen, did the same kindly. Their family documents exceeded what the earlier Memoir could use. Austen-Leigh traces the Austens and their Walters kin in Kent. Lincolnshire branches of the family enter the record as well. Letters carry much of Jane Austen's own quick, funny voice. Readers get the novelist's quiet life told by those who kept her papers.
22595-at-the-point-of-the-sword:
Herbert Hayens wrote At the Point of the Sword, a boys' adventure story set in old Peru. The catalog record gives no year. Hayens wrote many tales for young readers. Here he opens by teaching before he entertains. Peru, he explains, was once called the Land of the Sun, because its native people worshipped the sun.

The background runs to Cuzco, the great Inca city, and to Manco Capac, counted the first of the Inca emperors. Against that storied past of empire and conquest, the young hero's adventures play out. Boys of the era got history folded into their thrills. Modern readers get both a period adventure and a glimpse of how empire was romanticized for children.
22792-perils-and-captivity-comprising-th:
Perils and Captivity gathers true accounts of shipwreck and suffering, centered on the Picard family, French emigrants wrecked on the African coast in the disaster of the frigate Medusa. The catalog record names no author and gives no year. The Medusa's wreck in 1816, and the raft that became a byword for horror, shocked all Europe.

The narrative praises one young sufferer's amiable and girlish simplicity, which renders her story particularly engaging. It also reflects, with English satisfaction, that such disaster could not have befallen a British crew. The blame falls on the leaders' selfishness, aboard both ship and raft. That, the book argues, made the affair so serious. The volume belongs to the literature of maritime disaster, half testimony and half moral lesson, that the nineteenth century devoured.
22867-meeting-of-the-board:
Boardroom worry fills Meeting of the Board, a story of business under pressure. Walter, its central figure, sits with reports waiting on his desk. The promotion-draw reports and the expected dividend reports trouble him most. A shop steward goads him, annoying but tolerable. A man named Torkleson is a different matter.

The story stays close to office ground, where labor trouble and money trouble meet. Walter's weariness gives the piece its tone, a manager ground down between workers below and owners above. Nothing here needs a battlefield or a storm. The drama is fluorescent and familiar. Readers who enjoy workplace fiction from the industrial age will find a sharp little specimen, complete with period detail.
a-personal-record: Joseph Conrad's memoir of how a Polish boy became a British sea captain and then a great English novelist. With irony and feeling he recalls his years before the mast, the ships and shipmates who shaped him, and his anxious leap into writing. Short and beautifully composed, it is the most personal book by one of literature's great outsiders.
aristotle-complete-works-oxford:
Aristotle, Plato's pupil and teacher of Alexander the Great, wrote the body of works gathered here around 350 BC. The Oxford translation, edited under W. D. Ross, is the standard English Aristotle. The set holds 26 works drawn from the Internet Classics Archive at MIT, each by its noted translator.

The range is unmatched: logic, physics, metaphysics, ethics, politics, rhetoric, poetics, and a vast biology. His History of Animals alone fills a full study of creatures from direct observation. Aristotle built the first full system of Western thought, sorting every field into its own science. For two thousand years, students simply called him 'the Philosopher.'
beethoven-the-man-and-the-artist-as-reve: Beethoven speaks here in his own letters, notes, and sayings. The great composer shares his hopes, his deafness, and his fiery temper. Readers meet the man behind the mighty music. An intimate portrait drawn from his own hand.

A federal judge ordered the FBI to hand over its tapes and transcripts from the wiretapping of Martin Luther King Jr. Under the order, the material went to the National Archives, sealed for thirty years. The suit that forced the order was brought by Bernard Lee, a close King aide, and the Southern Christian Leadership Conference.

The FBI had recorded King for years, and what should happen to those recordings stayed in court long after his death. The order split the difference: the tapes were preserved, but locked away for a generation. The news report records the ruling, the archive named to hold the material, and the men and organization who won it.

juvenal-satires-persius-gifford:
Juvenal wrote sixteen fierce satires on Roman life around the early second century. Lewis Evans gave a literal prose version, and William Gifford added his famous verse rendering. Persius, Sulpicia, and fragments of Lucilius complete the volume.

Juvenal attacks corrupt nobles, greedy legacy hunters, and noisy city streets. His phrase about bread and circuses comes from these poems. Persius writes tighter, more Stoic satires on folly and freedom of mind. The Bohn Classical Library edition put both translators between one set of covers. Angry, funny, and often obscene, Roman satire here shows its full range and bite.
kilmeny-of-the-orchard:
Kilmeny of the Orchard is a novel by L. M. Montgomery, dedicated to her cousin Beatrice A. McIntyre. An epigraph from Hogg's Queen's Wake describes Kilmeny: still-faced, with a cheek like a moss rose. Her voice, the verse says, is like a distant melody. A verse from Kipling's The Light That Failed stands beside it.

Kilmeny is a Prince Edward Island girl who cannot speak, and her silence shapes the story. Eric Marshall, a young teacher, comes to her family's orchard world and learns her story. Montgomery, famed for Anne of Green Gables, gives this shorter novel the same island light. The epigraphs announce its mood: beauty, music unheard, and feelings words cannot carry.
looking-backward:
Edward Bellamy, an American writer, wrote this tale of a man who wakes in the year 2000, in 1888. Its full name adds the span 2000 to 1887, the year its hero falls asleep. The book sold in vast counts and set off a wave of clubs in its hero's name.

Julian West sleeps in a sealed room and wakes in a Boston made new and fair. Work, goods, and cash are shared by the state in a calm, planned scheme. The book gave the hope of a kind world a shape that men of its age could grasp.
lucretius-de-rerum-natura-leonard:
Lucretius, a Roman poet of the first century BC, wrote On the Nature of Things to free readers from fear. William Ellery Leonard's 1916 English translation renders the poem in strong blank verse. The poem teaches the system of Epicurus in six books of Latin verse.

Lucretius argues that all things are atoms and empty space, and that the gods take no part in human affairs. The soul, being atoms, ends at death, so death is nothing to fear. He treats the senses, the growth of human society, and the plague that struck Athens. The poem is both a physics and a cure for dread, and its science is startlingly modern in spirit.
lucy-raymond-or-the-children-s-watchword:
Lucy Raymond; Or, The Children's Watchword is a Canadian tale for the young. Agnes Maule Machar wrote it, as the author of Katie Johnstone's Cross. James Campbell and Son published it at Toronto. Chapters begin with Miss Preston's last Sunday and Lucy's home.

Nelly's Sunday evening, a strawberrying party, and a mission follow. Temptations, partings, and new experiences test the children. Lucy makes a start in life and learns what ambition costs. Friendship and faith guide her through each trial. The book belongs to the Sunday-school shelf of its day. It teaches kindness and trust in a gentle story form.
making-his-way-or-frank-courtney-s-strug:
Making His Way tells of Frank Courtney's struggle upward, by Horatio Alger, Jr. Whitman Publishing of Racine issued this boy's novel. Frank is a schoolboy when a telegram brings his bereavement. Mrs. Manning's will then leaves him disinherited and near penniless.

The Mannings' heir, Mark, yields to temptation and falls into trouble. Frank sets out for New York and seeks work in vain. A Wall Street adventure and a young tea merchant change his luck. He wins a place as a private secretary by honest merit. Alger's tale rewards pluck, temperance, and steady work. It is a classic sample of his rags-to-respectability stories.
martin-pippin-in-the-apple-orchard:
Eleanor Farjeon wrote Martin Pippin in the Apple Orchard as a prose fairy tale. J. D. Beresford wrote the foreword for American readers. He calls her gift rare, and ranks her with Stephens and de la Mare.

Beresford says five pages took him out of his tired work day. Sunlight, humor, and sweet surprise held him till the end. He wishes more readers the same joy, and trusts the tale to speak for itself from there. Beresford ranks the gift of true fairy tale above plain skill. He found that rare gift on show in her verse as well.
miracles-of-our-lord:
George MacDonald published these papers on the miracles of Jesus in 1870. He wrote them at request, he says, believing the miracles express Christ's unseen life. Since Christ came so that people may know God, MacDonald argues, every word and action of his matters. The chapters sort the miracles by kind.

MacDonald treats healings asked and unasked, miracles granted to friends' prayers, and the casting out of devils. Later chapters cover the raising of the dead, power over nature, and the Resurrection. He insists that believing in God makes the miracles no great extra strain. The book reads the Gospel wonders as theology in action.
nasa-tm-19690018395-a-comparison-of-thre:
Gerald E. Wilson, of Goddard's Laboratory for Theoretical Studies, compares three sets of higher order plasma equations. His paper, X-641-69-194, is dated May 1969, and he held a resident research associate post. Each set gives accurate approximate expressions for the average motion of a plasma. The plasma drifts in electric and magnetic fields that vary only slowly across it.

No inconsistencies are revealed by the comparison, Wilson shows. Two of the three techniques turn out to be completely equivalent. Most results of the third method can also be obtained from that equivalent pair. As a byproduct, the comparison yields a quantity that stays conserved along a particle's guiding center path. Chapters treat the Chew-Goldberger-Low theory and the guiding center plasma before the verdict.
nasa-tm-19710022798-piston-manometer-as-:
I Warshawsky of the Lewis Research Center wrote this paper for an October 1971 vacuum congress in Boston. It presents a piston manometer as an absolute standard for checking vacuum gauges. At very low pressures, gauges disagree unless one trusted reference exists. Warshawsky's device measures pressure directly from force and area. No other gauge is needed to set it.

A thin round disc hangs in a hole in the chamber wall, nearly filling it. Gas flows through the narrow gap around the disc to a pump. A balance weighs the force the gas presses on the disc. Known weights calibrate the balance in place. The device covered the range from ten to five hundred microtorr with small error.

oxford:
Andrew Lang, sometime fellow of Merton College, published his Oxford papers in a 1922 illustrated edition with color plates by George F. Carline. His preface disclaims any history of the university: these are merely records of the impressions made by this or that aspect of Oxford life as it has been in different ages.

Oxford, he writes, is not easy to design in black and white. On a wild winter day the sunshine fleets along the plain. Towers, floods, and trees gleam in watery light. Then the melancholy mist creeps back. The damp soaks into the heart of everything. Lang, novelist, folklorist, and classicist, writes of his own university as a lover sketches a face he knows too well to summarize.
peter-bell-the-third:
Percy Bysshe Shelley published Peter Bell the Third under the comic mask of Miching Mallecho, meaning mischief. The dedication, addressed to Thomas Moore under a playful name, introduces Peter Bell as the dullest of three Peter Bells. Wordsworth's Peter Bell poem had lately appeared, and Shelley's satire answers it.

Shelley's Peter changes colours like a chameleon and his coat like a snake: sublime, then dull, then prosy and dull, then ultra-legitimately dull. The poem follows him through respectability and religion into hell. It is Shelley's sharpest piece of literary mockery, aimed at a poet he thought had sold his gift.
polyaenus-stratagems-shepherd:
Polyaenus compiled his Stratagems of War in 162 CE for two Roman emperors. R. Shepherd's English translation appeared in 1793. The collection gathers some nine hundred stratagems from myth to Macedon.

Ambushes, feints, disguises, and mind games fill the eight books. Generals, kings, and even gods contribute their famous tricks. Polyaenus wrote for emperors marching to war against Parthia. He hoped past cleverness would inspire present victories on campaign. Shepherd's translation delivered the ancient handbook of battlefield cunning to English officers. Not every tale is true, and Polyaenus rarely cares. As a storehouse of military deception, the collection has no ancient rival. Kings, chiefs, and plain troops all get their due in its long lists of tricks.
prince-jan-st-bernard:
Forrestine C. Hooker wrote Prince Jan, St. Bernard, illustrated by Lynn Bogue Hunt and issued by Doubleday in a 1946 printing of her 1921 story. She dedicates the book to an American patriot, her father, Brigadier-General Charles L. Cooper, whose fifty-seven years of service ended at the last roll call in 1919. Her hero is a puppy of the Great St. Bernard Hospice, bred to the duty stated in the frontispiece caption: the duty of a St. Bernard is to save lives and be worthy of his ancestors.

Contents carry Jan from the hospice dogs and the land of snow to a new world and a land of no snow. California, where kindness fails and Jan learns to hate, lands in the pound, and must find his way back to his nature. Jan's trials teach the era's favorite lesson: breeding and duty will out.
songs-of-a-savoyard: The lyrics of W. S. Gilbert collected without Sullivan's music: the patter songs, the love ballads, the topsy-turvy choruses from the Savoy operas.
